questions.q: While writing about the land 2,000 years ago, Kavya keeps using the words 'Indian Subcontinent' instead of 'India'. Her friend asks why. Which reason fits the chapter best?
questions.a: The land then had different boundaries, not today's defined borders and states
o: The land then had different boundaries, not today's defined borders and states
The Subcontinent is the modern nation with defined states and a known population
People living there 2,000 years ago had no name at all for their land
'Subcontinent' is the name the Persians gave the land after taking the Indus region

questions.q: Arjun's chart says each ancient name of India is known from only one kind of source. Which name from the chapter shows that his chart is wrong, because it turns up in two different kinds of source?
questions.a: Jambudvipa: in the Mahabharata and in Ashoka's inscription
o: Jambudvipa: in the Mahabharata and in Ashoka's inscription
Sapta Sindhava: in the Rig Veda and in a Persian inscription
Hindustan: in a Persian inscription and in the Mahabharata
Bharata: in the Vishnu Purana and in a Greek inscription

questions.q: A class project collects four sources that name the land. Which one records a name given by visitors from outside rather than by the land's own inhabitants?
questions.a: A Persian stone inscription that calls the land 'Hidu'
o: A Persian stone inscription that calls the land 'Hidu'
Ashoka's inscription that calls the land 'Jambudvipa'
The Mahabharata's verse that uses 'Bharatavarsha'
The Vishnu Purana's verse that defines 'Bharata'

questions.q: A historian has two records about the land: one by people who lived there, one by a visitor who came from Iran. For the chapter's question 'What were the ancient names for India?', why is it useful to read both?
questions.a: Inhabitants and outside visitors used different names, so each record shows its own set
o: Inhabitants and outside visitors used different names, so each record shows its own set
A visitor's name is always more correct than the one used by the people who lived there
Only names used by inhabitants count as ancient names of the land
Both records are certain to give exactly the same name for the land

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the course of history, India has been called by many names.

Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about how we learn India's past names.
1. Some of India's names were given by its inhabitants and some by visitors from outside.
2. The chapter says the region looked the same 5,000 years ago as it does today.
3. Accounts of travellers and pilgrims are one source of India's ancient names.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Match each find in Column A with the kind of source in Column B.
Column A: 1. A verse in a very old poem that names the land  2. An emperor's message cut into a rock  3. A visiting monk's description of the places he saw  4. A 1950 document that spells out a nation's basic principles and laws
Column B: a. inscription  b. ancient text  c. account of a traveller or pilgrim  d. constitution
The chapter says the region was very different 500, 2,000 or even 5,000 years ago. Ashoka's inscription, of about 250 BCE, sits closest to the ___-year mark of these three.

The chapter opens with Sri Aurobindo's words about 'this great surge of humanity between the Himalayas and the two seas'. The Himalayas are the mountain wall along the north of the Subcontinent. Neha draws a sketch to match these words. Which sketch fits?
questions.a: Mountains across the north and sea on both sides of the southern land
o: Mountains across the north and sea on both sides of the southern land
Sea across the north and mountains on both sides of the southern land
Two rivers in the north and a single mountain range in the south
A desert in the north and mountains along the eastern and western coasts

questions.q: True or False? 'Some of the names of India that we know from the past were given by people who were not its inhabitants.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says India has been called by many names both by its inhabitants and by visitors from outside; for example, the Persians, who lived in Iran, called it 'Hind' or 'Hindu'.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: names came from visitors from outside too, with one example such as the Persians' 'Hindu'

questions.q: (a) A record of the name 'Hidu' was cut into stone on the orders of a Persian emperor. Say which of the chapter's kinds of source it is, and whether it shows a name given by the land's inhabitants or by visitors. (b) Ashoka's record of 'Jambudvipa' is the same kind of source. Explain why the two records still tell us different things about who named the land.
questions.a: (a) An inscription; it shows a name given by visitors from outside, since the Persians were the ancient inhabitants of Iran. (b) Ashoka was an Indian emperor, so his inscription records a name used by the land's own people, while the Persian one records an outsider's adaptation of 'Sindhu'. The kind of source and the question of who named the land are separate: one kind of source can carry an inhabitant's name or a visitor's name.
s: Part (a): inscription; a visitors' name (Persians from Iran)
Part (b): Ashoka's is an inhabitant's name, so the same kind of source can carry either; kind of source is not who named it

questions.q: (a) Name two things about India today that the chapter calls 'defined' or 'known'. (b) Using your answer, explain why a map of today's India would mislead someone studying the land 2,000 years ago.
questions.a: (a) Defined borders, defined states, a known population (any two). (b) Those borders and states belong to the modern nation; 2,000 years ago the region had shifting boundaries and other names, so today's lines would show divisions that did not exist then.
s: Part (a): any two of defined borders, defined states, known population
Part (b): those lines are modern; boundaries then were different and shifting

questions.q: Differentiate between names of India given by its inhabitants and names given by visitors from outside. Then place 'Sapta Sindhava' in the right group, even though it is built on the same river word as the Persian 'Hindu'.
questions.a: Inhabitants are people who live in a particular place; visitors came from outside the land (for example the Persians, who lived in Iran, and gave 'Hindu'). 'Sapta Sindhava' belongs with the inhabitants' names: it comes from the Rig Veda, India's own most ancient text. Sharing the root 'Sindhu' with 'Hindu' does not decide the group; who used the name does.
s: Meaning of each group (living in the land versus coming from outside)
Sapta Sindhava is an inhabitants' name (Rig Veda), because the group depends on who used it, not on the root

questions.q: Sri Aurobindo's words at the start of the chapter speak of the people 'between the Himalayas and the two seas'. (a) Which natural boundaries of the Subcontinent do these words point to? (b) Name the ancient source quoted later in the chapter that, like Aurobindo, speaks of seas on two sides of the land, and say which southern point it adds.
questions.a: (a) The Himalayas in the north and the seas on the two sides (east and west) of the southern land: the natural boundaries of the whole Subcontinent. (b) The poem of ancient Tamil literature (about 2,000 years old): it speaks of the oceans on the east and on the west, and adds Cape Kumari in the south (with the great mountain in the north).
s: Part (a): Himalayas in the north, seas on the east and west sides of the south
Part (b): the ancient Tamil poem, adding Cape Kumari in the south

questions.q: Ravi says: 'India today has defined borders, defined states and a known population, and its name has stayed India all through its history.' Is Ravi right? Give your verdict and the evidence for each half of what he says.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is right: the chapter says the India we know is a modern nation with defined borders, defined states and a known population. The second half is wrong: the land has had many names, such as 'Sapta Sindhava' for the northwest in the Rig Veda, 'Jambudvipa' and 'Bharata', and the name 'India' came only eventually, through the Persian 'Hindu' and the Greek forms 'Indoi'/'Indike'.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right half: modern nation with defined borders, states and a known population
Wrong half: many earlier names; 'India' came eventually through the Persian and Greek forms

questions.q: Kavya says: 'For each of its three kinds of source (ancient texts, inscriptions, accounts of travellers and pilgrims), the chapter quotes a name of the land.' Test her claim: give an example with its name for each kind where you can, and say what the chapter actually gives for the kind where you cannot.
questions.a: Partly right. Ancient texts: the Rig Veda gives 'Sapta Sindhava' (or the Mahabharata 'Bharatavarsha'/'Jambudvipa', the Vishnu Purana 'Bharata'). Inscriptions: Ashoka's inscription gives 'Jambudvipa' (or Persian stone inscriptions give 'Hind'/'Hidu'/'Hindu', or a Persian inscription gives 'Hindustan'). Travellers and pilgrims: the chapter tells of Xuanzang's journey (places visited, scholars met, Buddhist texts collected) but quotes no name of the land from his or any traveller's account; the Chinese 'Yintu'/'Yindu' come from 'several texts'. So the claim holds for two kinds, not the third.
s: Ancient text with the name it gives
Inscription with the name it gives
Travellers: Xuanzang's journey is told but no name is quoted from a traveller's account, so the claim is only partly right

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is 'an inscription'. Write a quiz question about the names of India that has this answer, and support it with two details from the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: 'In what kind of source did Emperor Ashoka use the name Jambudvipa for the whole of India?' Details: Ashoka, about 250 BCE, left many inscriptions; in one he used 'Jambudvipa' for India, which then included today's Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan. (Another valid question: the kind of source in which the Persians first wrote 'Hind' or 'Hindu', or in which 'Hindustan' first appeared.)
s: A question whose only answer is an inscription
First supporting detail from the chapter (who made it and when)
Second supporting detail (the name it records)

questions.q: Justify the statement: 'Both the boundaries and the names of India have changed over history.' Use at least two examples for boundaries and two for names.
questions.a: Boundaries: today India is a modern nation with defined borders and states, but the chapter says it was very different 500, 2,000 or 5,000 years ago. In Ashoka's time (about 250 BCE) the India he called 'Jambudvipa' included today's Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan. The Rig Veda's 'Sapta Sindhava' covered only the northwest. Names: the Rig Veda used 'Sapta Sindhava'; the Mahabharata used 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Jambudvipa'; later 'Bharata' became the common name; the Persians said 'Hindu', the Greeks 'Indoi', which led to 'India'. So the land, its limits and its names have all shifted.
s: Boundary example 1: modern defined borders versus a very different past
Boundary example 2: Ashoka's Jambudvipa included Bangladesh, Pakistan, parts of Afghanistan
Name example 1 from inhabitants (Sapta Sindhava, Bharatavarsha, Jambudvipa or Bharata)
Name example 2 from visitors (Hindu, Indoi or India)
Conclusion tying boundaries and names together

questions.q: Analyse how the names given to India by its inhabitants differ from the names given by visitors from outside. (a) Give two names from each group and where each came from. (b) Identify the one river name that sits at the root of names in BOTH groups, and give one name from each group built on it.
questions.a: (a) Inhabitants: 'Bharata' (from a Vedic group of people; defined in the Vishnu Purana) and 'Jambudvipa' (island of the jamun fruit; Mahabharata, Ashoka). Visitors: 'Hindu' (Persian adaptation of 'Sindhu') and 'Indoi'/'Indike' (Greek, from Persian sources, dropping the 'h' of 'Hindu'). (b) 'Sindhu', the Indus. From inhabitants: 'Sapta Sindhava' in the Rig Veda. From visitors: 'Hindu', 'Indoi', 'Yindu' or 'Tianzhu'.
s: Part (a): two inhabitant names with their origins
Part (a): two visitor names with their origins
Part (b): Sindhu (the Indus) as the shared root, with one name from each group

questions.q:
A Class 6 group is making a poster for the chapter's Big Question 'How do we define India?' about the land 2,000 years ago. They can print only one map. Ishaan wants a map of today's countries of the Subcontinent, so the poster can show how far Ashoka's 'Jambudvipa' reached. Zoya wants a physical map showing only mountains, rivers and seas, labelled 'Indian Subcontinent'.
(a) Using one ancient description of the land from the chapter, name the features Zoya's map must show in the north and the south.
(b) What fact about Ashoka's Jambudvipa would Ishaan's map show well?
(c) What could each map make a reader believe wrongly about the land 2,000 years ago?
(d) Decide which map to print, and say what the poster must add in words to make up for what that map loses.
questions.a: (a) The Vishnu Purana describes Bharata as north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains: the Himalayas in the north and the ocean in the south (the Tamil poem's great mountain in the north and Cape Kumari in the south also earn the mark). (b) That Jambudvipa included what is today Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan, besides today's India. (c) Ishaan's map shows today's defined borders, which did not exist then: the chapter says the region had shifting boundaries and was very different 2,000 years ago. Zoya's map shows no link to today's countries, so a reader could think the ancient land was the same as India today. (d) Zoya's physical map: the chapter's ancient definitions are drawn by natural limits, and modern borders would show divisions that did not exist. Its cost is that it hides how far Jambudvipa reached, so the poster adds a caption that Ashoka's Jambudvipa covered today's India, Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan.
s: Part (a): snowy mountains (Himalayas) north, ocean south, from an ancient description
Part (b): Jambudvipa included today's Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan
Part (c): one risk for each map (modern borders that did not exist; no link to today's countries)
Part (d): physical map, with a caption giving Jambudvipa's extent

questions.q:
Riya collects four items for a project on India's ancient names.
Item P: words carved on stone by an Indian emperor about 250 BCE that use the name 'Jambudvipa'.
Item Q: a verse from India's most ancient text naming the land of seven rivers.
Item R: an early Persian stone record calling the land 'Hidu'.
Item S: a Chinese text calling the land 'Yindu'.
(a) Which two items come from foreigners, and which two from inhabitants of India?
(b) Which two items are inscriptions?
(c) Item R comes from soon after the Persian campaign of the 6th century BCE. Taking it as 550 BCE, about how many years older is it than Item P?
(d) Riya's label reads 'A name Indians themselves used for the whole land'. Which single item fits, and why does the other inhabitants' item not fit?
questions.a: (a) Foreigners: R (Persian) and S (Chinese). Inhabitants: P (Ashoka) and Q (Rig Veda). (b) P and R. (c) 550 - 250 = 300 years older. (d) Item P: Ashoka used 'Jambudvipa' for the whole of India. Item Q is also Indian but 'Sapta Sindhava' names only the northwest region.
s: Part (a): R and S from foreigners, P and Q from inhabitants
Part (b): P and R are inscriptions
Part (c): about 300 years
Part (d): Item P; Q covers only the northwest

questions.q:
Read this leaflet handed out on a heritage walk in a town of the northwest of the Subcontinent.
Leaflet: 'Sentence 1: Our region was called Sapta Sindhava in the Mahabharata, India's most ancient text. Sentence 2: The name means "the land of the seven seas". Sentence 3: Much later, the Persians adapted the word Sindhu into "Hindu". Back page: Sapta Sindhava, the name of all India!'
(a) Correct the mistake in Sentence 1.
(b) Correct the mistake in Sentence 2, using where the word 'Sindhava' comes from.
(c) Sentence 3 is accurate. What did 'Hindu' mean in ancient Persian?
(d) The town wants to name its heritage walk with a Rig Veda name. Some prefer 'Bharata', the better-known name today; others prefer 'Sapta Sindhava'. Decide which suits a walk through this region, weighing what each word meant in the Rig Veda.
questions.a: (a) The name comes from the Rig Veda, which is India's most ancient text, not the Mahabharata. (b) It means 'the land of the seven rivers': 'Sindhava' comes from 'Sindhu', the Indus River or a river in general, not a sea. (c) It was a purely geographical term for the land of the Indus region, not a reference to the religion. (d) 'Sapta Sindhava': in the Rig Veda it is the name of this northwest region, a land. In the Rig Veda 'Bharata' was the name of one of the main Vedic groups of people, not of a land, and today it names all of India, so using it for one region would fit neither meaning. The cost is that 'Bharata' is far better known to visitors, so the walk's leaflet should explain the older name.
s: Part (a): the Rig Veda, not the Mahabharata
Part (b): seven rivers, since Sindhu means the Indus or a river
Part (c): a purely geographical term, not the religion
Part (d): Sapta Sindhava, since Bharata named a people in the Rig Veda (and now names all India); notes the cost

questions.q: A tour guide in Kerala tells visitors, 'The Rig Veda called our land Sapta Sindhava.' Which correction, based on the chapter, should a student offer?
questions.a: The Rig Veda used that name only for the northwest of the Subcontinent
o: The Rig Veda used that name only for the northwest of the Subcontinent
The name was given by Persian visitors after their campaign, not by the Rig Veda
Sapta Sindhava was Ashoka's name for the whole of India
The name means 'island of the jamun fruit', not a region

questions.q: Vivek's map labelled 'Sapta Sindhava' shows the Indus and two other rivers. Going by what the name means, ___ more rivers are missing from his map.
questions.a: four

questions.q: In an old verse, Tanvi reads that 'the sindhu flowed past the village', but the village lay far from the Indus. Which idea from the chapter explains this?
questions.a: 'Sindhu' could at times mean any river, not only the Indus
o: 'Sindhu' could at times mean any river, not only the Indus
The verse must be wrong about where the village was
'Sindhu' always meant the Indus River and never any other river
'Sindhu' was a Persian word for the snowy mountains

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Rig Veda's name 'Sapta Sindhava' is a name built on rivers.
Reason (R): 'Sindhava' comes from 'Sindhu', which refers to the Indus River or at times to a river in general.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
1. The Rig Veda is younger than Ashoka's inscriptions.
2. 'Sapta Sindhava' is the Rig Veda's name for the northwest region of the Subcontinent.
3. The word 'Sindhu' always meant the Indus River and never any other river.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: Sameer finds the word 'Sindhu' hidden inside the Rig Veda's name 'Sapta Sindhava'. Which later name for India, from the chapter, grew out of the same word?
questions.a: 'Hindu', used by the Persians
o: 'Hindu', used by the Persians
'Jambudvipa', used by Ashoka
'Bharatavarsha', used in the Mahabharata
'Bharatam', used in south India

questions.q: Kabir has two cards, 'Sapta Sindhava' and 'Hidu', and must say which name came from India's own people. Which reasoning is correct?
questions.a: Sapta Sindhava, as it comes from the Rig Veda; Hidu is a Persian adaptation
o: Sapta Sindhava, as it comes from the Rig Veda; Hidu is a Persian adaptation
Hidu, as the Persians reached the Indus before the Rig Veda was composed
Both, as both names are built on the same word, 'Sindhu'
Neither, as 'Sindhu' itself was a word from the Persian language

questions.q: Ashoka lived about 250 BCE. The chapter calls the Rig Veda India's most ancient text, several thousand years old. So, compared with Ashoka's inscriptions, the Rig Veda is the ___ source.
questions.a: older

questions.q: Meera writes that the name 'Bharata' was first coined by the Vishnu Purana. Which correction does the chapter support?
questions.a: It first appears in the Rig Veda, for one of the main Vedic groups of people
o: It first appears in the Rig Veda, for one of the main Vedic groups of people
It first appears in the Rig Veda, as the name of one of the seven rivers
It first appears in Ashoka's inscription, as the name of the jamun tree
It first appears in the Mahabharata, as the name of a snowy mountain in the north

questions.q: True or False? 'In the name Sapta Sindhava, the word Sindhava has nothing to do with the river word Sindhu; the two only look alike.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says 'Sindhava' comes from 'Sindhu', which refers to the Indus River or at times to a river in general. That is why 'Sapta Sindhava' means 'the land of the seven rivers'.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: Sindhava comes from Sindhu (the Indus or a river), giving 'land of the seven rivers'

questions.q: Asha says 'Sapta Sindhava' is the name of a river. Babu says it is the name of a land. (a) Who is right? (b) Using the word 'Sindhava', explain how Asha could have been misled.
questions.a: (a) Babu: 'Sapta Sindhava' means the land of the seven rivers, a name for the northwest region. (b) 'Sindhava' comes from 'Sindhu', which is a river name (the Indus, or a river in general), so Asha took the river word inside the name for the meaning of the whole name.
s: Part (a): Babu, with the meaning 'land of the seven rivers'
Part (b): the root 'Sindhu' is a river word, which misled Asha

questions.q: The chapter says 'Sindhu' refers to the Indus River, 'or at times to a river in general'. Write two sentences about an imaginary journey, one using 'Sindhu' in the first sense and one in the second sense.
questions.a: Sample: 'The traders crossed the Sindhu, the great river of the northwest, on rafts.' (Indus sense) 'In the hills they rested beside a small sindhu, a stream that fed the fields.' (any river sense) Any pair where one clearly means the Indus and the other means some river other than the Indus earns both marks.
s: A sentence where Sindhu clearly means the Indus River
A sentence where sindhu means a river in general, not the Indus

questions.q: (a) A student says 'Sapta Sindhava' and 'Jambudvipa' were named the same way. Show that they were not, by saying what each name is built on. (b) Which of the two came to mean the whole Subcontinent, and what does that show about naming a land after a single feature?
questions.a: (a) 'Sapta Sindhava' is built on rivers ('the land of the seven rivers', from 'Sindhu'); 'Jambudvipa' is built on a tree ('the island of the fruit of the jamun tree'). (b) 'Jambudvipa' came to mean the Indian Subcontinent, so a name taken from one feature, a common tree native to India, could still stand for a whole land; the river name in the Rig Veda stayed the name of one region.
s: Part (a): rivers for Sapta Sindhava, the jamun tree for Jambudvipa
Part (b): Jambudvipa came to mean the Subcontinent, so one feature can name a whole land

questions.q: (a) In the Rig Veda, what did the word 'Bharata' refer to? (b) How had its use widened by the time the Mahabharata spoke of 'Bharatavarsha'?
questions.a: (a) One of the main Vedic groups of people. (b) 'Bharatavarsha' means 'the country of the Bharatas', and in the Mahabharata it extends to the entire Subcontinent, so a group's name had become part of a name for the whole land.
s: Part (a): one of the main Vedic groups of people
Part (b): country of the Bharatas, covering the entire Subcontinent

questions.q: Dev says: 'The name Sapta Sindhava shows that the people of the Rig Veda named a region after its rivers.' Do you agree? Give your verdict and two reasons.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. 'Sapta Sindhava' means 'the land of the seven rivers', and 'Sindhava' comes from 'Sindhu', the Indus River or a river in general. The name is given to a region, the northwest of the Subcontinent, so a region was named after its rivers.
s: Verdict: agrees
The name means land of the seven rivers, from Sindhu (river)
It is the name of a region, the northwest

questions.q: Show that 'Sapta Sindhava' cannot be a name given by Persian visitors. Use three points from the chapter.
questions.a: 1. It comes from the Rig Veda, an Indian text, so it was used by the land's own people. 2. The Rig Veda is India's most ancient text; the Persians reached the Indus region only in the 6th century BCE. 3. The Persians' own forms of 'Sindhu' were 'Hind', 'Hidu' or 'Hindu', not 'Sindhava'.
s: Source is the Rig Veda, an Indian text
The Rig Veda is older than the Persian arrival in the 6th century BCE
The Persian forms were Hind/Hidu/Hindu, not Sindhava

questions.q: A student concludes: 'The people of the Rig Veda knew nothing of the land outside the northwest, because the Rig Veda's name Sapta Sindhava covers only the northwest.' Is this conclusion safe? Explain in three points.
questions.a: No, the conclusion is not safe. The chapter tells us that the Rig Veda gives the northwest the name 'Sapta Sindhava'. A name for one region does not prove that the people knew nothing beyond it; the chapter says nothing about what they did or did not know. A fair statement is only that this Rig Veda name covers the northwest, not the whole land.
s: Verdict: the conclusion is not safe
The chapter says only that the Rig Veda names the northwest
Naming one region is no proof of knowing nothing else; states the fair conclusion

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: 'The story of India's names begins with one river and ends with the same river.' Trace the beginning, trace the end, and say whether the claim is fully right.
questions.a: Beginning: the earliest name in the chapter is the Rig Veda's 'Sapta Sindhava', from 'Sindhu', the Indus River or a river in general. End through foreigners: the Persians adapted 'Sindhu' into 'Hind'/'Hindu'; the Greeks dropped the 'h' to get 'Indoi'/'Indike'; this led to English 'India'. So one ending does go back to the same river. But the other ending is 'Bharata', which goes back to a Vedic group of people, not a river; it became the name of India in most Indian languages and stands in the Constitution as 'India, that is Bharat'. So the claim is only partly right.
s: Beginning: Sapta Sindhava from Sindhu in the Rig Veda
Chain Sindhu to Hindu to Indoi to India
Bharata comes from a Vedic group of people, not a river
Bharata is still in use and in the Constitution
Judgement: partly right, with reason

questions.q: The chapter's two Big Questions are 'How do we define India?' and 'What were the ancient names for India?' Evaluate how far the Rig Veda helps to answer each one.
questions.a: Names: it helps a great deal. It gives the earliest name in the chapter, 'Sapta Sindhava'; its word 'Sindhu' is the root later used by Persians, Greeks and Chinese; and the name 'Bharata' first appears in it, for a Vedic group, later leading to 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Bharata'. Defining India: it helps only a little. Its name covers only the northwest region, so it cannot tell us the limits of the whole land; for that the chapter turns to the Mahabharata, Ashoka's inscription and the Vishnu Purana. Overall the Rig Veda is strong on names and weak on defining the whole land.
s: Earliest name, Sapta Sindhava
Sindhu as the root of later foreign names
Bharata first appears in it
Limit: it covers only the northwest, so it cannot define the whole land
Overall judgement for each Big Question

questions.q:
Three cards are found in a box labelled 'One word, three peoples'. Card X reads 'Sindhu'. Card Y reads 'Hindu'. Card Z reads 'Indoi'. A note says each card was written by a different people, and each form grew out of an earlier card.
(a) Arrange the cards from the oldest form to the newest.
(b) Working backwards from Card Z, name who made each change and what changed.

questions.q:
Match each name in Column A with the kind of name it is in Column B.
Column A: 1. Kaccha  2. Bharatavarsha  3. Jambudvipa  4. Sapta Sindhava
Column B: a. a name for one region, more or less today's Kutch  b. a name for the whole land, from a group of people  c. a name for the whole land, from a tree  d. a name for one region, from its rivers
True or False? 'Because Jambudvipa means an island, Ashoka must have used the name for an island off the coast, not for the mainland.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. 'Jambudvipa' means 'the island of the fruit of the jamun tree', but the name came to mean the Indian Subcontinent. Ashoka used it to describe the whole of India, which then included what is today Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the name came to mean the Subcontinent; Ashoka used it for the whole of India

questions.q: True or False? 'Because the Mahabharata names separate regions such as Vanga and Kerala, it had no name for the Subcontinent as a whole.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. Besides its many regions, the Mahabharata uses 'Bharatavarsha', which clearly extends to the entire Subcontinent, and 'Jambudvipa', which came to mean the Indian Subcontinent.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: it also uses Bharatavarsha (and Jambudvipa) for the whole Subcontinent

questions.q: (a) What does 'Bharatavarsha' mean? (b) A student says the name must honour one particular king called Bharata. Using the chapter, explain why this cannot be settled so simply.
questions.a: (a) 'The country of the Bharatas'. (b) 'Bharata' first appears in the Rig Veda as the name of one of the main Vedic groups of people, and later literature mentions several kings named Bharata, so the name cannot be pinned on one particular king.
s: Part (a): the country of the Bharatas
Part (b): Bharata was first a Vedic group, and there were several later kings of that name

questions.q: (a) Besides today's India, which present-day countries had land inside the Jambudvipa of Ashoka's inscription? (b) Use this to explain what the chapter means by India's 'shifting boundaries'.
questions.a: (a) Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan. (b) Land that Ashoka named as one, 'Jambudvipa', now lies in four different countries, so the limits of what was called India have changed over time.
s: Part (a): Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan
Part (b): one named land is now spread over several countries, so the limits changed

questions.q: Differentiate between the two kinds of names the Mahabharata uses for places, giving an example of each.
questions.a: It names many separate regions, many of them also kingdoms, such as Kashmira, Vanga or Kaccha, each covering a part of the land. It also uses names for the entire Subcontinent, 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Jambudvipa'.
s: Region names for parts of the land, with an example
Names for the whole Subcontinent: Bharatavarsha and Jambudvipa

questions.q: (a) Write the meaning of 'Jambudvipa' as the chapter gives it, and say which word in that meaning describes a kind of land. (b) Using the chapter's description of the jamun tree, suggest why a tree could give its name to a whole land.
questions.a: (a) 'The island of the fruit of the jamun tree'; the word 'island' describes the land. (b) The chapter says the jamun is a common tree native to India, so a tree found widely across the land could stand for the whole land, and 'Jambudvipa' came to mean the Indian Subcontinent.
s: Part (a): island of the fruit of the jamun tree; 'island' is the land word
Part (b): a common tree native to India, found across the land

questions.q: Kiran claims: 'The Mahabharata's region names tell us exactly where each region's borders lay, just like a modern map of states.' Do you agree? Give your verdict and two reasons.
questions.a: No. The chapter gives only rough modern equivalents: Kashmira is 'more or less' Kashmir, Kurukshetra 'parts of' Haryana, Pragjyotisha 'roughly' Assam. Also, ancient Indian texts are difficult to date and the region's boundaries have shifted over history, so exact borders cannot be read from the names.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Modern equivalents are only rough (more or less, parts of, roughly), with an example
Texts are hard to date and boundaries shifted

questions.q: Nandini claims: 'Jambudvipa and Bharatavarsha both appear in the Mahabharata, and both are named after a tree.' Judge her claim. Give your verdict and the evidence for each half.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is right: the Mahabharata uses both 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Jambudvipa'. The second half is wrong: only 'Jambudvipa' comes from a tree ('the island of the fruit of the jamun tree'); 'Bharatavarsha' means 'the country of the Bharatas', and 'Bharata' first appears in the Rig Veda as one of the main Vedic groups of people.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right half: both names are in the Mahabharata
Wrong half: only Jambudvipa is from a tree; Bharatavarsha is from the Bharatas, a Vedic group of people

questions.q: Write a three-sentence description of the land that a visitor of about 250 BCE might give, which fits Ashoka's Jambudvipa but would NOT fit India today. Each sentence must use a fact from the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: 'The people of this land call it Jambudvipa, after the fruit of the jamun tree. Their emperor, Ashoka, uses that name on his inscriptions for all the land he describes. It stretches over what will one day be Bangladesh and Pakistan and into parts of Afghanistan.' The third sentence is what makes it fit Ashoka's Jambudvipa and not present-day India.
s: Uses the name Jambudvipa with its jamun-fruit meaning
Links it to Ashoka's inscription of about 250 BCE
Includes land now in Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan

questions.q: The chapter's text names six Mahabharata regions: Kashmira, Kurukshetra, Vanga, Pragjyotisha, Kaccha and Kerala. Use these positions of modern places: Kashmir and Haryana lie in the north, Bengal and Assam in the east, Kutch in the west, Kerala in the far south. Sort the six Mahabharata regions into north, east, west and south through their modern equivalents. What does this spread suggest about the text?
questions.a: North: Kashmira (Kashmir), Kurukshetra (parts of Haryana). East: Vanga (parts of Bengal), Pragjyotisha (roughly Assam). West: Kaccha (Kutch). South: Kerala. The regions are spread across the whole land, which suggests the Mahabharata's list covers the entire geography of the Subcontinent.
s: North and east regions placed correctly
West and south regions placed correctly
Conclusion: the list covers the entire Subcontinent

questions.q: Compare and analyse 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Jambudvipa' under these heads: meaning, what each name grew out of, the sources the chapter finds each in, the area each covered, and which kind of name, 'Jambudvipa' or 'Bharata', became the common one later.
questions.a: Meaning: Bharatavarsha is 'the country of the Bharatas'; Jambudvipa is 'the island of the fruit of the jamun tree'. Origin: Bharata was first a Vedic group of people in the Rig Veda; Jambudvipa comes from a common tree native to India. Sources: both are in the Mahabharata; Jambudvipa is also in Ashoka's inscription of about 250 BCE. Area: both stood for the entire Subcontinent; Ashoka's Jambudvipa included today's Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan. Later: a few centuries later 'Bharata' became the name generally used, and today it is the name of India in most Indian languages.
s: Meanings of both names
Origins: a people versus a tree
Sources: Mahabharata for both, Ashoka's inscription for Jambudvipa
Area: both the whole Subcontinent, with Ashoka's extent
Bharata became the common name

questions.q: Justify: 'For knowing WHEN Jambudvipa meant the whole land, Ashoka's inscription is more useful than the Mahabharata; for knowing the land's REGIONS, the Mahabharata is more useful than Ashoka's inscription.'
questions.a: When: the Mahabharata uses 'Jambudvipa', but ancient texts are hard to date and it was written 'from a few centuries BCE onward', so it gives no firm date. Ashoka's date is about 250 BCE, and his inscription uses 'Jambudvipa' for the whole of India, so it fixes a time by which the name meant the whole land. Regions: the Mahabharata lists many regions such as Kashmira, Kurukshetra, Vanga, Pragjyotisha, Kaccha and Kerala, covering the entire Subcontinent, with numerous rivers and peoples. The chapter takes from Ashoka's inscription only the name and the land it covered (including today's Bangladesh, Pakistan, parts of Afghanistan), not a list of regions. So both halves of the statement hold.
s: Mahabharata cannot be dated firmly
Ashoka's inscription gives about 250 BCE for Jambudvipa as all of India
Mahabharata lists regions across the Subcontinent, with examples
Ashoka's inscription gives the name and extent, not regions
Conclusion that both halves are justified

questions.q:
A museum is setting up a gallery called 'One Name for the Whole Land'. Its draft labels read:
Card 1: Kaccha  |  modern place: ______
Card 2: Vanga  |  modern place: ______
Card 3: 'Jambudvipa' in Emperor Ashoka's inscription, about 250 BCE  |  map: ______

(b) Which present-day countries, besides India, should the map on Card 3 shade?
(c) Cards 1 and 2 name single regions. Explain why the curator still finds them useful in a gallery about a name for the whole land.
(d) There is room for one more card: 'Bharatavarsha' or a second card on the meaning of 'Jambudvipa'. Decide which to add, and name what the gallery loses by your choice.
questions.a: (a) Kaccha: today's Kutch; Vanga: parts of Bengal. (b) Bangladesh, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan. (c) They are part of the Mahabharata's long list of regions, which together cover the entire geography of the Subcontinent; so the same text that knew the whole land also uses names for all of it. (d) 'Bharatavarsha': it is a second name for the entire Subcontinent, from the same text as Cards 1 and 2, and it leads to 'Bharata', the later general name. The loss: it has no firm date like Ashoka's (the Mahabharata is placed only 'from a few centuries BCE onward'), and visitors do not get the jamun-tree meaning of 'Jambudvipa'.
s: Part (a): Kutch and parts of Bengal
Part (b): Bangladesh, Pakistan, parts of Afghanistan
Part (c): the regions in the list together cover the whole Subcontinent
Part (d): Bharatavarsha, a second whole-land name, with the loss named

questions.q:
A theatre group is writing a play set in the world of the Mahabharata. The narrator must use the text's own names. In one scene the heroes travel from Kaccha to Pragjyotisha. (Kutch lies in the far west of India today and Assam in the far northeast.)
(a) Which two names for the whole land could the narrator take from the Mahabharata?
(b) Which of these two names did an emperor also use in an inscription, and about when?
(c) Using the modern equivalents of the two regions, explain what the heroes' journey tells the audience about the land the text knew.
(d) The play's title must be 'Jambudvipa' or 'Bharatavarsha'. The director wants audiences today to link the ancient name with a name they still use. Decide, and say what the other title would have offered.
questions.a: (a) 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Jambudvipa'. (b) 'Jambudvipa', used by Ashoka, about 250 BCE, for the whole of India. (c) Kaccha is today's Kutch and Pragjyotisha roughly today's Assam, so the journey crosses the land from the far west to the far northeast: the text's regions span the whole Subcontinent, not one corner. (d) 'Bharatavarsha': it is 'the country of the Bharatas', and 'Bharata' later became the general name, still used today as 'Bharat'/'Bharatam' and in most Indian languages. 'Jambudvipa' would have offered a name with a firm date from Ashoka's inscription and the jamun-tree meaning, but the chapter shows no link from it to a name in use today.
s: Part (a): Bharatavarsha and Jambudvipa
Part (b): Jambudvipa, Ashoka, about 250 BCE
Part (c): Kutch to Assam, west to northeast, so the text knew the whole land
Part (d): Bharatavarsha for the link to Bharat today, naming what Jambudvipa offered

questions.q: Compare and analyse the Vishnu Purana's description of Bharata with the ancient Tamil poem's description of the land. Cover: the limits each gives, what each is actually describing, what they share, what the Tamil poem adds, and what the chapter concludes from the two together.
questions.a: Limits: the Vishnu Purana calls Bharata the country north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains; the Tamil poem (about 2,000 years old) speaks of Kumari in the south, the great mountain in the north and the oceans on the east and west. What they describe: the Vishnu Purana defines the land itself; the Tamil poem praises a king whose name is known across this stretch. Shared: a mountain in the north and the sea in the south. Added: the Tamil poem also names the oceans on the east and west and the southern point, Cape Kumari. Conclusion: different parts of the country adopted a similar definition of India, and ancient Indians knew their geography well.
s: Limits in the Vishnu Purana
Limits in the Tamil poem, and that it praises a king
Shared limits: mountain in the north, sea in the south
Tamil poem adds east and west oceans and Kumari
Conclusion: similar definition in different parts; good knowledge of geography

o: A land lying north of the snowy mountains

questions.q: True or False? 'A description that names only a mountain range in the north and an ocean in the south can still cover the whole Subcontinent.' Give the verdict and an example from the chapter.
questions.a: True. The Vishnu Purana does exactly this: it calls Bharata the country north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains, and that takes in the whole land lying between them, the entire Subcontinent.
s: Verdict: True
Example: the Vishnu Purana's ocean-and-snowy-mountains definition covers all the land between

questions.q: (a) Which name, according to the chapter, became the one generally used for the Indian Subcontinent a few centuries after Ashoka's time, and which ancient text does the chapter quote for it? (b) Riya says this name survives today only in the Constitution. Give two pieces of evidence from the chapter that prove her wrong.
questions.a: (a) 'Bharata'; the Vishnu Purana. (b) Any two: it is generally written 'Bharat' in north India and often 'Bharatam' in south India; the chapter's summary says it is the name of India in most Indian languages; it 'remains in use even today'.
s: Part (a): Bharata, quoted from the Vishnu Purana
Part (b): two pieces of present-day use besides the Constitution

questions.q: (a) Identify the 'snowy mountains' of the Vishnu Purana. (b) Is its brief description of Bharata correct for the land? Give your verdict with a reason.
questions.a: (a) The Himalayas. (b) Yes, broadly correct: the land does lie between the Himalayas in the north and the ocean in the south, and the ancient Tamil poem marks out the same northern mountain and southern sea, which shows ancient Indians knew their geography well.
s: Part (a): the Himalayas
Part (b): broadly correct, the land lies between the Himalayas and the southern ocean

questions.q: The ancient Tamil poem praises a king, not the land. Explain how it still gives us a definition of the land.
questions.a: It says the king's name is known from Kumari in the south, the great mountain in the north and the oceans on the east and west. These four limits mark out the whole stretch of land, so in praising the king's fame the poem also draws the land's boundaries.
s: States the four limits named in the poem
Explains that these limits outline the extent of the land

questions.q: (a) The chapter calls a constitution a document that spells out the basic principles and laws of a nation. Using this, explain why it matters that 'India, that is Bharat' stands right at the beginning of India's Constitution. (b) In which two languages does the chapter show this phrase, and how do the two versions differ in the order of the names?
questions.a: (a) The nation's own basic document gives both names at its very start, so 'Bharat' is officially kept as the country's name alongside 'India'. (b) English, in which the Constitution was first written: 'India, that is Bharat' (India first). Hindi: 'Bharat arthath India' (Bharat first).
s: Part (a): the basic document itself keeps both names, so Bharat is official
Part (b): English puts India first, Hindi puts Bharat first

questions.q: Asha claims: 'Two ancient sources from different parts of India drew the limits of the land in much the same way, so ancient Indians shared a clear picture of their land.' Do you agree? Give your verdict and two reasons.
questions.a: Yes. The Vishnu Purana describes Bharata as the land north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains. A poem of ancient Tamil literature, about 2,000 years old, speaks of Kumari in the south, the great mountain in the north and the oceans on the east and west. The chapter itself says different parts of the country adopted a similar definition and that ancient Indians knew their geography well.
s: Verdict: agrees
Vishnu Purana and Tamil poem limits compared
The chapter's own conclusion: similar definitions, good knowledge of geography

questions.q: Show that the Vishnu Purana's 'Bharata' cannot be just another name for the Rig Veda's 'Sapta Sindhava'. Give three points.
questions.a: 1. Area: Sapta Sindhava is the northwest region only; Bharata is the whole country north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains. 2. Meaning: Sapta Sindhava means 'land of the seven rivers'; Bharata goes back to a Vedic group of people and 'the country of the Bharatas'. 3. Source and time: Sapta Sindhava is from the Rig Veda, India's most ancient text; Bharata became the general name for the land only later ('a few centuries later', after Ashoka's time).
s: Different areas: northwest versus the whole land
Different meanings: seven rivers versus the Bharatas
Different sources and times

questions.q: Sunil says: 'Bharat is a name that only north Indians use; south Indians never use it.' Judge his claim. Give your verdict and two reasons.
questions.a: No. 'Bharat' is only the spelling generally used in north India; in south India the same name is often written 'Bharatam'. The chapter's summary also says 'Bharata' is the name of India in most Indian languages, so south Indians do use it.
s: Verdict: disagrees
The south uses the same name, written 'Bharatam'
Bharata is the name of India in most Indian languages

questions.q: Justify: 'Bharata is the name that links India's most ancient text to its modern Constitution.' Trace at least four steps.
questions.a: 1. 'Bharata' first appears in the Rig Veda, India's most ancient text, as the name of one of the main Vedic groups of people. 2. The Mahabharata uses 'Bharatavarsha', the country of the Bharatas, for the entire Subcontinent. 3. A few centuries later 'Bharata' became the name generally used for the land; the Vishnu Purana defines it as the country north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains. 4. It remains in use: 'Bharat' in the north, 'Bharatam' in the south, and in most Indian languages. 5. The Constitution, in force from 1950, opens with 'India, that is Bharat'. So the same name links the two, though its meaning widened from a people to the whole land.
s: Rig Veda: Bharata as a Vedic group
Mahabharata: Bharatavarsha for the whole Subcontinent
Vishnu Purana: Bharata as the general name with its limits
Present use: Bharat, Bharatam, most Indian languages
Constitution's opening phrase, with the meaning widening from a people to the land

questions.q:
A school is making a poster titled 'Bharata: how ancient Indians defined their land'. It has room for ONE quotation, and the designer wants the quotation itself to contain the name in the title. The choice is between the Vishnu Purana's verse and a poem of ancient Tamil literature, about 2,000 years old, which praises a king whose name is known 'from [Cape] Kumari in the south, from the great mountain in the north, from the oceans on the east and on the west...'
(a) Name the 'great mountain in the north'.
(b) Which two limits do the two sources share?
(c) Say one thing each source does that the other does not.
(d) Decide which quotation suits this poster, and say what the poster loses by leaving the other out.
questions.a: (a) The Himalayas. (b) A mountain in the north (the snowy mountains) and the sea or ocean in the south. (c) The Vishnu Purana names the land, 'Bharata', and gives a definition of it; the Tamil poem gives limits on all four sides, including the oceans on the east and west and Cape Kumari, but it praises a king rather than naming the land. (d) The Vishnu Purana: the quotation must contain the name in the title, and only this verse uses the name Bharata in a definition. It loses the east and west limits and the proof, from a Tamil poem, that a different part of the country adopted a similar definition.
s: Part (a): the Himalayas
Part (b): mountain in the north, ocean in the south
Part (c): Vishnu Purana names and defines Bharata; the poem gives four limits while praising a king
Part (d): Vishnu Purana for the poster's title, naming what is lost

questions.q:
For Republic Day, a school in Mysuru puts up three cards.
Card A: 'India, that is Bharat'  (language: ________)

questions.q:
A quiz club in Madurai builds a timeline of the name Bharata. Its items: Ashoka's inscription (about 250 BCE); the Tamil poem praising a king (about 2,000 years ago); the Vishnu Purana's verse on Bharata; the Constitution of India (in force from 1950).

(b) Which of the four items use the name Bharata for the land, and which item only describes the land's limits without naming it?
(c) The club wants to place the Vishnu Purana exactly. Explain why it can only be placed roughly.
questions.a: (a) Ashoka's inscription comes first: 250 BCE is 250 years before the Common Era began, and the Common Era is itself already a little over 2,000 years old, so the inscription is about 2,275 years old, older than the poem's 2,000 years by roughly 275 years. (b) The Vishnu Purana and the Constitution use 'Bharata'/'Bharat' for the land; the Tamil poem describes the limits (Kumari, the great mountain, the eastern and western oceans) without giving the land a name, and Ashoka's inscription uses another name, 'Jambudvipa'. (c) The chapter gives no date for the Vishnu Purana; it says only that 'a few centuries later' Bharata became the general name and quotes the Vishnu Purana as an example, and it warns that ancient Indian texts are difficult to date. So it can be placed only roughly, some centuries after Ashoka's time.
s: Part (a): Ashoka's inscription first, about 2,275 years old against about 2,000
Part (b): Vishnu Purana and Constitution name Bharata; the Tamil poem only gives limits
Part (c): no date given, only 'a few centuries later', and ancient texts are hard to date

(d) A page of the translated manuscripts: the title is about what China took home, and he collected Buddhist texts and translated them into Chinese. The loss: visitors do not see what the Chinese called India, 'Yindu', or that the name goes back to 'Sindhu'.
s: Part (a): 7th century, 17 years, Xuanzang
Part (b): translated them from Sanskrit into Chinese
Part (c): many Chinese scholars came over the centuries, so it was not a one-off
Part (d): the translated page, naming what the panel loses

questions.q:
A school in Hyderabad is naming its new magazine. The shortlist: 'Bharati' (from Bharata), 'Jambu' (from Jambudvipa) and 'Indica' (from the Greek Indike).
(a) For each of the three root names, say whether it was given by India's inhabitants or by foreigners.
(b) Which root name, according to the chapter's summary, became widespread, and how widespread is it today?
(c) Which root name goes back to the river Sindhu, and through which people did it reach the Greeks?
(d) The school wants a name that readers across India will recognise and that comes from the land's own people. Decide, and say what the other inhabitants' name would have offered.
questions.a: (a) Bharata and Jambudvipa: India's inhabitants; Indike: foreigners (the Greeks). (b) Bharata; it is the name of India in most Indian languages. (c) Indike: it goes back to 'Sindhu' through the Persians, whose sources the Greeks used, dropping the 'h' of 'Hindu'. (d) 'Bharati': it comes from an inhabitants' name that became widespread and is used in most Indian languages. 'Jambu' would have offered the jamun-tree meaning and a name with a firm date, used in Ashoka's inscription of about 250 BCE for the whole of India.
s: Part (a): Bharata and Jambudvipa from inhabitants, Indike from foreigners
Part (b): Bharata, the name in most Indian languages
Part (c): Indike, from Sindhu through the Persians
Part (d): Bharati, naming what Jambu would have offered
